- P-175 **On the compiled path a call's arguments run in parallel where `ParallelismAnalyzer` judges them worth a task, as a tuple's elements do, so a reduction's two halves run in parallel; the one library's parallel range stops its split at a grain size, not at single elements.** The one library's range joins a reduction's halves as the arguments of one call, `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))`, and splits down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1308-1342`); the code generator evaluates a call's arguments in order (F-19, row 951), under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???" (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:7068`), so every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of microGPT would run its bodies one at a time once compiled programs run the one library. The split stops at a chunk that runs efficiently in sequence: in his words, "you need the right forking constants", as Steele's parallel trees end in sequential leaves and Clojure's persistent vectors take their branching factor from B-trees. It needs a group of forked arms to join every arm before it completes abruptly, which the compiled path does not do (`CodeGen.genParallelExprs` joins on the normal path only, row 947; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 7.1). The library binding the halves as a tuple, and reductions left in sequence, are declined. Why: the specification evaluates each argument of a call in an implicit thread of its own (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex:60-64`), walk forks a call's arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:342`), and the model's parallelism is its reductions (the review, section 6). POSITIONS.md:76

The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two are on a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85; F-333). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. POSITIONS.md:110
- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The suites and the gate

POSITIONS.md:130
- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
